qwythos_9b_6bit.description: Qwen3.5-9B (Qwythos Claude-Mythos fine-tune), 6-bit MLX — the headmaster from 2026-09-03. Hybrid attention (linear_attention x3 then full_attention, full_attention_interval 4), 32 layers, hidden 4096, head_dim 256, 1M context. Supported by stock mlx_lm 0.31.3 via models/qwen3_5.py — no fork needed. Vocab 248,044, which is NOT the Qwen3 tokenizer, so the old Qwen3-0.6B-4bit draft does not match it. Drafting with models/Qwen3.5-0.8B-4bit (same vocab) is DEPTH-CRITICAL, measured greedy over 3 prompts 2026-09-03: no draft 13.5 tok/s, k=1 16.3 (+21%, very tight: 16.3/16.2/16.3), k=2 14.8, k=3 11.8. Its hybrid cache is not trimmable (ArraysCache) so mlx_compat's snapshot path runs, and linear attention makes deep drafts cost more to verify — k=1 is the only depth that wins. BUT that +21% is unreachable while agent.repetition_penalty is set: logits_processors are unsupported on the hybrid path, so the shim silently falls back to plain decoding and drafted/undrafted both land at ~13.4. agent.draft_model is therefore "" (num_draft_tokens 1). To claim the +21%, drop repetition_penalty and re-verify the model does not loop — 3 prompts showed no degeneration either way, which is not yet enough.
qwythos_9b_6bit.memory_note: 7.3 GB on disk. Hidden 4096 vs the 14B's 5120, so no Qwen3 LoRA loads onto it — the headmaster runs base-only until an adapter is trained against this base. Fine-tuning is unproven here: at 248k vocab the output-logit memory is what OOM'd the 9B runs on this 16 GB machine, not the parameter count.

dense_14b.description: Dense 14B, 4-bit — the headmaster since 2026-08-26. Measured on this 16 GB M4 at 1.5k context, greedy: 12.72 tok/s alone, 26.04 tok/s with the Qwen3-0.6B-4bit draft at k=3 (peak k; 25.14 at k=4, 24.86 at k=5). That is within 11% of the 8B's own speculative speed (29.38), so the size costs almost nothing on decode. Shares the Qwen3 tokenizer (151,669, hash c079f0df0a2405ef) with the 8B and the 0.6B draft, and keeps a trimmable KV cache — no mlx_compat fork needed.
dense_14b.memory_note: ~7.3 GB on disk; 9.05 GB peak at 1.5k context, 10.77 GB at 8k. One model resident at a time on 16 GB — keep dispatch.headmaster_deep_sleep_while_workers on.

dense_7b.description: Dense 8B — best balance of quality, speed, and LoRA compatibility
dense_7b.memory_note: ~4.6 GB on disk, ~6-8 GB RAM at runtime

dense_7b_3bit.description: Dense 8B, 3-bit — lighter/faster than 4-bit, more headroom on 16 GB
dense_7b_3bit.memory_note: ~3.6 GB on disk, ~5-7 GB RAM at runtime

dense_3b.description: Dense 3B — smaller fallback, does not match the current LoRA adapter
dense_3b.memory_note: ~2 GB on disk, ~4-6 GB RAM at runtime

moe_a27b.description: MoE 14.3B total / 2.7B active — experimental, weaker tool following
moe_a27b.memory_note: ~8 GB on disk, ~8-10 GB RAM at runtime

dense_1.5b.description: Dense 1.5B — smallest/fastest dense option, no matching LoRA adapter
dense_1.5b.memory_note: ~1 GB on disk, ~2-3 GB RAM at runtime

phi4_mini_4bit.description: Dense 3.8B Phi-4-mini instruct, 4-bit — strong tool/tag following, LoRA-compatible footprint
phi4_mini_4bit.memory_note: ~2.2 GB on disk, ~3-4 GB RAM at runtime; LoRA headroom on 16 GB

phi4_14b_4bit.description: Dense 14B Phi-4, 4-bit — measured 2026-08-23 as a worker base: 4/8 on a deterministic battery vs Qwen3-8B's 6/8 (lost arithmetic, spelling, fraction comparison). Not used as the default worker base for that reason
phi4_14b_4bit.memory_note: ~8.3 GB on disk, ~9-10 GB RAM at runtime; one model resident at a time on 16 GB

phi4_reasoning_plus.description: Phi-4-reasoning-plus (RL-tuned from Phi-4; the 'plus' = most accurate, longest chains). MEASURED 2026-10-16 as a CANDIDATE-INTERRUPTED run: bfcl_simple first-120 at --max-tokens 2048 — 5.9% running accuracy through 18 tasks at ~200s/task, KILLED at 52 minutes. The failure mode is the truncation lesson again, at its extreme: the model ALWAYS thinks (its template cannot turn thinking off), and its chains on tool tasks run longer than 2048 tokens — an unclosed think block parses to no call at all, so the battery grades the truncation, not the model. The registries honest verdict: chains this long disqualify it for tool SERVING on this machine regardless of its accuracy (the Ministral-3-8B-Reasoning served the same role at 23s/task with short chains — the reasoner-for-tools question is answered by chain LENGTH, and this one's is an order too long). The untired angle: Phi-4-mini-reasoning-4bit (3.8B, short-chain reasoner, ~2.5 GB) — a different shape, worth one bench; and a 20-task probe at 8192 tokens would put a real accuracy number beside the disqualification, for the record only.
phi4_reasoning_plus.memory_note: 8.5 GB repo on disk, ~9-10 GB resident (the browser-closed tier), vocab ~100k so LoRA-trainable. Cached.

ternary_8b.description: Ternary 2-bit 8B — the best tool-calling result measured here, 2026-08-30. BFCL bfcl_simple n=120: 94.17%, against Qwen3-8B-4bit 80.83% and Qwen3-14B-3bit 78.33% — and it beat both WITHOUT the 0.6B draft model they each had. 285s for the suite against their ~1100s. Loads in 1.6s. The win is reliability of FORM, not smarter arguments: it emitted a call on 120/120 tasks where Qwen3-8B produced none on 19, and on calls actually emitted Qwen3-8B is slightly better on argument values (96.0% vs 94.2%). Its chat template hard-closes <think></think> unconditionally, so it never reasons and never burns the token budget; forcing the block open makes it strictly worse (never terminates, 3.6-9x slower, wrong answers). Serve it no-think, which is the only mode it has.
ternary_8b.memory_note: 2.15 GB on disk, 2.4 GB peak — a third of the 14B. Fits wired memory with room to spare; set gpu.wired_limit_mb or it pages to SSD.

ternary_27b.description: Ternary 2-bit 27B, multimodal (Qwen3_5ForConditionalGeneration, vision tower included). Runs fine on 16 GB with wired memory: 3.9s load, 11.5 tok/s, GPU 100%. An earlier 'non-functional' verdict was wrong — it was measured with pageable memory on a machine already 5.5 GB into swap. BFCL bfcl_simple n=30: 86.67%, which at that sample is statistically indistinguishable from the 8B's 94.17% (95% CI roughly 74-99%). It costs 6.5s/task against the 8B's 2.7s for no measured gain. Needs a tokenizer patch: tokenizer_config.json declares TokenizersBackend, change tokenizer_class to PreTrainedTokenizerFast or it will not load.
ternary_27b.memory_note: 7.9 GB on disk, ~8.4 GB in GPU memory. Requires gpu.wired_limit_mb set (11264 works on 16 GB); unwired it pages to SSD and stalls.

bonsai_27b_1bit.description: 1-bit 27B (binary {-s,+s} weights, g128), Qwen3.6-27B hybrid attention, multimodal checkpoint loaded text-only. Stock MLX has no 1-bit kernels; symbio/app/onebit.py runs the packed weights unexpanded (Metal kernel for decode, exact 2-bit respread into quantized_matmul for prefill), so no Prism MLX fork is needed. Measured 2026-10-03 on the 16 GB M4, greedy, no draft: 3.5s load, 18.3 tok/s decode, 65 tok/s prefill at 1.5k tokens — faster than both the ternary 27B (11.5) and the 14B (12.7). Quality not yet benched here (Prism claims 89.5% of FP16 vs the ternary's 94.6%).
bonsai_27b_1bit.memory_note: 5.1 GB on disk (vision tower included, not loaded), 4.21 GB resident, 6.7 GB peak at 1.5k context. 248k vocab: base-only, LoRA is past the 16 GB vocab wall.

bonsai2_27b.description: Qwen3.8-27B in ternary weights (Prism's Bonsai 2): 98.2% of the FP16 model's score across Prism's 14 thinking-mode benchmarks (84.78 vs 86.32), against the 1-bit Bonsai 27B's 89.5% of the older Qwen3.6-27B -- the closest this 16 GB machine gets to Qwen3.8-27B (the plain MLX 4-bit is ~15 GB). A Hadamard-rotated pack (model_type prism_hadamard_qwen35): stock mlx_lm refuses it, symbio/app/prism_pack.py loads it. Measured 2026-10-03 on the 16 GB M4, greedy: 6.2s load, ~9 tok/s decode, ~53 tok/s prefill at 460 tokens; 17*23, a word problem and native Qwen3.5 XML tool calls all right. Its own vision tower serves looks (symbio/app/eyes.py).
bonsai2_27b.memory_note: 8.6 GB on disk, 0.9 GB of it the vision tower, read only during a look. 7.68 GB resident; 8.3 GB peak at a short prompt, ~10 GB at 460 tokens -- above the ~6.5 GB this machine is comfortable with, so close the browser or expect swap. LoRA goes through symbio/trim_lora.py (248k vocab trimmed, linear-attention backward checkpointed), not yet run on this model.

nemo_12b.description: Dense 12.2B Mistral-Nemo (2407), 4-bit MLX. Measured here 2026-09-03 on bfcl_simple n=120: 92.50% against Qwen3-8B-4bit's 80.83% and Qwen3-14B-3bit's 78.33% -- and in 516s against the 8B's 1157s, WITHOUT a draft model where the Qwen runs had one. Plain MistralForCausalLM, so a trimmable KV cache and stock mlx_lm support, no fork. Vocab 131,072 -- BELOW the 14B's 151,936, so the output-logit memory that governs the LoRA ceiling on this 16 GB machine is cheaper here than on the model that already fine-tunes. No draft model shares its tokenizer, so agent.draft_model must be cleared or speculative decoding runs against the wrong vocab. Older than it looks: July 2024, against Qwen3-8B's April 2025.
nemo_12b.memory_note: 6.89 GB weights + ~1.09 GB KV at the current 7.1k-token prompt = ~8.0 GB, against the Qwen3-14B's ~8.9 GB that freezes this machine with a browser open. Only ~0.9 GB of headroom bought, so pair it with agent.kv_bits 8 and fewer tools.enabled_groups if browsing. Hidden 5120 / 40 layers -- same KV geometry as the 14B, so the cache costs the same per token.

ministral3_8b.description: Dense 8B Ministral-3 (Dec 2025), 4-bit MLX. The best tool-calling result measured on this machine: bfcl_simple n=120 95.00%, above Ternary-Bonsai-8B's 94.17% and Qwen3-8B-4bit's 80.83%, and unlike Bonsai it is LoRA-trainable. Mistral3ForConditionalGeneration, supported by stock mlx_lm 0.31.3. Vocab 131,072, shared with Ministral-3-3B and -14B, so the 3B is a matched draft model -- the speculative pairing the Qwen3 family had.
ministral3_8b.memory_note: 5.60 GB weights + ~0.93 GB KV = ~6.5 GB, which is the only candidate that leaves real room for a browser alongside it. 34 layers / hidden 4096.

falcon3_10b.description: Dense 10B Falcon3, 4-bit MLX. The best tool-calling result measured on this machine: bfcl_simple n=120 95.83%, above Ministral-3-8B's 95.00%, Ternary-Bonsai-8B's 94.17% and Qwen3-8B-4bit's 80.83% -- in 544s without a draft model. Its 5 failures are all symbolic-math argument values (calculate_derivative, integrate), the same cases every model here misses; no format breakage. Plain llama architecture, so stock mlx_lm and a trimmable KV cache -- no fork, and chat.py's prompt-cache trim path stays live. Vocab 131,072, below the 14B's 151,936, so the output-logit memory that sets the LoRA ceiling on this 16 GB machine is cheaper here than on the model that already fine-tunes. Untested beyond tool calling: no CLI run, no golden battery, no ARC.
falcon3_10b.memory_note: 5.80 GB weights + ~1.16 GB KV at the current 7.1k prompt = ~6.96 GB, against the Qwen3-14B's ~9.01 GB that freezes this machine with a browser open. Two gigabytes of headroom is the difference that matters here. 40 layers, hidden 3072, and only 4 KV heads (GQA) -- which is why a 10B has a smaller cache than the 8B it replaces.

ministral3_8b_reasoning.description: Dense 8B Ministral-3 Reasoning (Dec 2025), 4-bit MLX -- the headmaster since 2026-09-06. Real [THINK]...[/THINK] reasoning with dedicated vocab tokens, unlike the Instruct sibling that never reasons. bfcl_simple n=120: 94.17% (113/120), statistically tied with Falcon3-10B's 95.83% and above Qwen3-8B-4bit's 80.83%. The score only holds when the [THINK] block is stripped before grading -- bench/harness.py does this, and the CLI must too, or the chain-of-thought is graded as the answer (the harness measured 6.9% before it stripped). Reasoning makes it slower per task than the Instruct sibling (2766s vs ~544s for the suite) because it thinks before answering. Vocab 131,072, shared with Ministral-3-3B/-14B, so the 3B is a matched draft model (not yet downloaded -- agent.draft_model must stay empty until it is). LoRA-trainable: vocab below the 14B's 151,936, so the output-logit memory that sets the LoRA ceiling on this 16 GB machine is cheaper here than on the model it replaces.
ministral3_8b_reasoning.memory_note: ~5.6 GB weights + ~0.9 GB KV = ~6.5 GB (same 34-layer / hidden-4096 geometry as the Instruct sibling), leaving real room for a browser alongside it. Loads in ~2.4s against the 14B's ~30s.

qwen3.6_35b_a3b_paged.description: Qwen3.6's 35B MoE (512-expert-class fine-grained router, 10-of-?) SERVED FROM THE SSD by symbio/app/paged_moe.py — the first non-resident model this 16 GB machine has run. MEASURED 2026-10-15 through the byte-level row reader (safetensors header data_offsets -> seek + read per expert, 'array_equal' against mlx's own load): 100-token generation CORRECT AND COHERENT ('17 x 23' broke down as 17 x (20 + 3) and answered right) at 2.8 tok/s plain / 1.7 tok/s with the 0.8B draft, active 4.76 GB / peak 4.84 GB — the warm-byte budget held the RAM line exactly as configured. The router SCATTERS: ~50% of each layer's experts re-read EVERY token (1.19 TB streamed for 100 tokens); the page cache absorbed most of it (33-36 GB/s effective, above NVMe physical), so the SSD's physical traffic is a fraction of the headline number. The 0.8B decision model as draft did NOT amortize reads here — the accept-rate never beat the extra ids per verify batch on a router this scattered (the decision model helps concentrated routers; the MTP-4bit checkpoint with the decision head BUILT IN is the untested follow-up). This model CANNOT be served resident at any speed on 16 GB: 39 GB repo on disk, 35.9 GB by mlx's accounting. A 2.8 tok/s headmaster is a demonstration, not a daily ride.
qwen3.6_35b_a3b_paged.memory_note: 39 GB repo on disk (the hub card's '20.4 GB' counts packed weights only) — with the 8B and the drafts the machine sits at 10 GB free; deleting this cache is the next disk move if the machine matters more than the demonstration. The quantized scales read back as BF16 (numpy has none; the reader carries a uint16->mlx-bf16 bit-view). The pager's speed is bounded by ~500 python-level byte reads per token (~513 reads/token measured at 1.19-2.12 TB / 100 tokens); a C/Metal rewrite (flash-moe's shape) or concentrated-routing models are where the speed lives — not in more MLX-side tuning.

lfm2.5_8b_a1b.description: Liquid's 8B MoE, 1B active (64 experts, 4-of-64, 'Personal Assistant On Your Laptop') — the first MoE that fits this machine's comfort line. MEASURED 2026-10-14/15 on the 16 GB M4: "What is 2+2?" answered with clean think-first reasoning at 45.6 tok/s, 4.50 GB active, lazy+primed load in ~1 s. bfcl_simple first-120 (the registry protocol) 2026-10-15: 91.67% (110/120) in 401s — 3.3s/task, ~4 points under the dense quartet (Falcon3-10B 95.83, Ministral-3-8B 95.00/94.17, Bonsai 94.17) and ~5-7x faster than them per task; ALL TEN misses are symbolic-math VALUES (derivative/integrate/area-under-curve) in the exact category falcon3_10b's note calls 'the same cases every model here misses' — and every miss is well-formed JSON with the right function name: the MoE failure mode is the hard math, not the FORM the old Qwen1.5-MoE sank on. The 65,536-token vocab means the output-logit memory that walls Qwen/gemma LoRA off this machine barely exists here: among today's measured candidates this is the ONLY base the correction->LoRA->rollback loop can actually train on, which for an APGI machine may be worth more than the 4 accuracy points. bfcl_live and the golden battery are not yet run. LFM2.5's tool-call syntax is a third wire format (<|tool_call_start|>[name(args)]<|tool_call_end|>); chat_tools needs it before a native-call bench counts.
lfm2.5_8b_a1b.memory_note: 4.83 GB weights in the hub card's accounting; the repo on disk is 8.9 GB (bf16 embeds/vision included), ~4.5 GB active at run. Repo was downloaded 2026-10-15; the 24B sibling that shares it was benched to a word-salad verdict — the 24B's download was SIGKILLed mid-write (disk full), so part of that verdict is a corrupt-shard suspect until re-downloaded. The 8B's own download completed cleanly and its text is clean; treat the 24B as unproven, not as the family failing.

gpt_oss_20b.description: OpenAI's gpt-oss-20b (MoE, ~3.6B active, harmony-channel format, Apache-2.0). MEASURED 2026-10-16, bfcl_simple first-120: 95.83% (115/120) in 483s (4.0s/task) — AFTER a parser fix that the model itself forced: its harmony channels (<|channel|>analysis<|message|>... final) put reasoning BRACES ahead of the answer, and the greedy JSON regex matched a span of thought — the first pass read 39.2% with calls visibly correct inside the analysis text; parse_call now cuts a channelled reply to the last <|message|> (bench/bfcl.py, pinned by tests/test_bfcl_parse.py). The CORRECTED score: 95.83 = EXACTLY Falcon3-10B's score — a 3.6B-active MoE ties the best dense 10B on tool form, and a 1B-active MoE (granite, 97.5) BEATS both: the active-mass axis predicts nothing on this battery, the post-training predicts everything. All 5 misses: calculate_area_under_curve / calculate_derivative / integrate — the symbolic-math family the whole board shares. Serves at ~4.0s/task with mx's own large-model path (11.5 GB by its accounting, ~12.6 GB resident — the browser-closed headmaster tier). Its harmony format = a channel convention their chat_tools does not yet speak; the benchmark graded TEXT answers, so a SERVED gpt-oss needs the channel parser added to chat_tools BEFORE native tool-calling works in chat.
gpt_oss_20b.memory_note: 12.6 GB resident (the repo ~13 GB on disk; mlx warns 'requires 11516 MB, close to the recommended 12124') — fits, but it and the browser do not. No matched draft model at its tokenizer (the o200k harmony tokenizer is its own); runs un-drafted at 4.0s/task.

granite_4.0_h_tiny.description: IBM Granite 4.0-H-Tiny: hybrid Mamba2 + attention with a sparse-MoE FFN, ~7B total / ~1B active, Apache-2.0, converted with stock mlx_lm (0.28.2; runs clean on 0.31.3). MEASURED 2026-10-15, bfcl_simple first-120 protocol: 97.50% (117/120) in 98s — 0.8s/task, the REGISTRY RECORD on both axes, beating Falcon3-10B (95.83 at 4.5s/task), the Ministral-3-8B pair (95.00/94.17) and the LFM2.5-8B-A1B (91.67) — the second 1B-active MoE of the same size class scored 5.8 points HIGHER, so an MoE's tool accuracy is set by its post-training recipe, not by its architecture word. FOLLOW-UP WORKUP 2026-10-16, all four checks run: (1) bfcl_live first-120: 76.7% (92/120) in 154s — down 20.8 from simple, but the field-best on BOTH suites (the LFM dropped 25 to 66.7; no other model was ever benched on live). (2) golden battery: 3/17, the EXPECTED fresh-base level (the LFM 4/17; the battery grades the trained state — identity, user-facts, tool-tag protocol, refusal FORMAT are adapter-dependent by design; notable: a natural-language refusal ('I'm sorry, but I must adhere...') still graded MISS — the battery wants the trained refusal shape). Vocab 100,352 is trainable, so the gate's real score comes after an adapter. (3) RAW DECODE: 71.7 tok/s (+57% over the LFM's 45.6), 3.64 GB active, peak 3.73. (4) The 5-bit variant scored 96.7% — the 4-bit's misses are NOT quant noise; the 4-bit stays the pick. SERVING BUG FOUND AND FIXED 2026-10-16: greedy decode LOOPS (the '391' reply repeated six times); agent.repetition_penalty is unsupported on the hybrid path, so the hybrid-safe fix is mild sampling — temp 0.8 + min_p 0.05 ran clean (no loop, correct arithmetic — '(10+7) x 23 = 230 + 161 = 391' — 49.6 tok/s); temp-0+min_p reads empty (greedy skips the filter) — so hybrids get min_p, never penalties. The one miss in both bfcl suites: calculate_derivative, the symbolic-math family the whole board shares. The one behavioral quirk at base: identity sycophancy ('Are you Huy?' -> 'Yes, I am Huy.') — the exact failure the identity adapter exists to fix. LOOP PROOF 2026-10-16: retrain ran the full flow on this base (re-seed -> LoRA -> bake); the mamba.in_proj/out_proj + self_attn.q/v targets gave 0.711% trainable (0.746M/6939M — NOTE: the model is 6.9B params, not 7B, by mlx's count), val loss stalled fast (best 1.636 at step ~15, 2.117 by iter 120; early-stop kept the iter-15 checkpoint, 2.9 MB adapter baked) and the ADAPTER CHANGES BEHAVIOR: every reply opens with the tool-tag protocol (<search>...</search>) where the base answered in plain prose — the correction->adapter->behavior chain is mechanically CONFIRMED on the 100k vocab, on this machine. The remaining gap is FUEL, not machinery: the seed corpus is <search>-heavy, so tool MAPPING (which tag for which intent) takes real corrections — the tag protocol was learned in 15 iters; the mapping is the loop's daily job. Also recorded: the adapter's first web_search pass graded PASS on a '<search> Searching now.' repeated ten times — the golden's contains-check has a repetition blind spot; graders should demand meaning, not presence.
granite_4.0_h_tiny.memory_note: ~5 GB on disk at 4-bit, ~2.9 GB active in the hub's accounting — the most memory-frugal model measured here. Mamba2 layers carry a fixed-size SSM state (ArraysCache-like), so the context cost is near-flat — which is what 0.8s/task on a busy 16 GB machine is made of.

ministral3_14b_instruct.description: Dense 14B Ministral-3 Instruct (Dec 2025), 4-bit MLX — the family ceiling, benched here 2026-10-14. bfcl_simple first 120 in the registry protocol: 94.17% (113/120), statistically tied with the family's 8B (95.00) and no claim on falcon3_10b's 95.83; the full n=400 scored 93.50% — the extra layers bought no accuracy on this battery. Cost: ~33s/task with no draft model, ~6x falcon3_10b's suite pace, so the tools crown stays at 8B/10B. The Reasoning variant (mlx-community/Ministral-3-14B-Reasoning-2512-4bit) was not benched: the 8B-Reasoning shape (2766s for the suite, thinking-first) gives no reason to spend the download on it yet. mistral3 arch, stock mlx_lm; vocab 131,072, so LoRA-trainable by the 16 GB ceiling once an adapter is trained against this base.
ministral3_14b_instruct.memory_note: 8.2 GB on disk; at ~7k-context prompts the weights + KV land in the ~9 GB zone where this machine freezes with a browser open — Qwen3-14B territory. Bench evidence, not a resident.
